translations.title: Southbound Vs Northbound Freight And The Border Handoff Explained
translations.excerpt: Southbound freight goes US to Mexico; northbound goes the other way. Here is how the border handoff works and what changes by direction.
translations.content:
Southbound freight moves from the US into Mexico; northbound freight moves from Mexico into the US. The core difference is which country's customs clears the load and which documents lead. In both directions the trailer is handed off at the border by a transfer (drayage) tractor while customs is processed. For a southbound load through Laredo with complete paperwork, clearance is usually same day and delivery to Monterrey takes 1 to 2 business days.

  • Southbound is US to Mexico and clears through Mexican customs (SAT) with a pedimento; northbound is Mexico to US and clears through US customs (CBP).
  • In both directions a transfer tractor performs the border handoff; it is a short move, not the long haul.
  • A well documented southbound FTL load from Laredo reaches Monterrey in 1 to 2 business days.
  • Laredo is North America's busiest inland port, with more than 17,000 trucks crossing per day (City of Laredo, 2026).

What's the difference between southbound and northbound freight?

Direction and which customs clears it. Southbound goes US to Mexico and clears Mexican customs with a pedimento; northbound goes Mexico to US and clears US customs.

The terms simply describe direction, but the paperwork and the clearing authority change with it. Southbound freight travels from the US into Mexico, so it clears through Mexican customs (SAT) and a licensed customs broker files the pedimento. Northbound freight travels from Mexico into the US, so it clears through US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) with a US entry. If you are an e-commerce seller or importer sending inventory into Mexico, you are almost always dealing with southbound freight. Knowing which side leads matters because it decides which documents are critical and which broker you need. BringGo Ship runs southbound freight daily through its Laredo and Monterrey warehouses with a licensed Mexican customs broker.

How does the border handoff work?

A transfer (drayage) tractor takes the trailer across the border while customs is processed. It is a short, dedicated move between the two sides, not the long haul.

At the border the trailer does not simply drive straight through; it is handed off. A transfer or drayage tractor picks up the trailer on one side and drops it on the other while the customs paperwork is processed. On a southbound load, the trailer leaves the US warehouse, US export formalities are completed, the transfer tractor moves it to the Mexican side, the broker releases the pedimento, and a domestic carrier takes it onward. This handoff is short by design, but it is a real step, and coordinating it with the customs release is what keeps a load from sitting in a yard. When the transfer and the clearance are managed together, the trailer moves as soon as it is legally cleared.

What documents differ by direction?

Southbound leads with the Mexican import set: pedimento, commercial invoice, HS codes, certificate of origin and Carta Porte. Northbound leads with a US entry.

The document that leads depends on which customs clears the load. For southbound freight into Mexico, the driving documents are the commercial invoice, packing list, correct HS codes, the certificate of origin for the USMCA rate, and the Complemento Carta Porte for the Mexican road leg; the broker uses these to file the pedimento. In 2026 the certificate of origin must be uploaded digitally before shipment or you lose the preferential rate. For northbound freight into the US, the load clears with a US entry through CBP. Because most importers moving inventory into Mexico deal with southbound freight, the Mexican import set is the one to master first.

How long does each direction take?

With complete paperwork, a southbound crossing usually clears same day. Total transit from Laredo to Monterrey is 1 to 2 business days; interior points add 2 to 4 days.

Direction affects the paperwork more than the clock; what drives time in either direction is documentation and inspection. For a southbound load through Laredo with complete, consistent documents, clearance is usually same day and delivery to Monterrey takes 1 to 2 business days. Interior destinations like Mexico City add 2 to 4 days of domestic transport. A red light inspection (rojo) on the Mexican side adds 1 to 2 days. Season matters too: around El Buen Fin in November and the December peak, the bridge and customs get busier, so leave a 2 to 3 day buffer. The table below summarizes the southbound timeline through Laredo.

What slows the handoff down?

Documents, almost always. An invoice that does not match the pedimento, a wrong HS code, or a missing Carta Porte turns a same day crossing into a multi day wait.

The handoff itself is quick; what slows a crossing is the paperwork around it. On southbound freight, the top causes of delay are an invoice that does not match the pedimento, an incorrect HS code, and a missing Complemento Carta Porte. A missing or late certificate of origin costs you the USMCA rate. Under the 2026 reform, the importer and broker share liability for the declaration, so accuracy is more valuable than ever. Timing adds risk too: a trailer that reaches the border late on a Friday can sit through the weekend. The fix is to verify every document while the freight is still at the warehouse, so the handoff and clearance flow without a pause.

Step or routeTypical time

Laredo to Monterrey (FTL)1 to 2 business days
Laredo to Mexico City (FTL)3 to 5 business days
Red light inspection (rojo) added1 to 2 days

Definitions

  • Southbound freight: Southbound freight is cargo moving from the US into Mexico, cleared through Mexican customs with a pedimento.
  • Transfer or drayage: The transfer is the short move that hands the trailer from one side of the border to the other during clearance.

Frequently asked questions

Is my e-commerce inventory southbound or northbound?

If you are sending inventory from the US into Mexico, it is southbound and clears through Mexican customs with a pedimento. Northbound is the opposite direction, into the US. Most sellers stocking the Mexican market deal with southbound freight.

Do I need two brokers for a round trip?

Directionally, yes: southbound clears through a Mexican customs broker, and northbound clears through a US entry with CBP. Each leg has its own documents and clearing authority, even if the physical lane is the same.

What is the driver handoff at the border?

It is the transfer step: a dedicated tractor moves the trailer from one side of the border to the other while customs is processed, instead of a single driver going straight through. It is short but necessary for the clearance to happen.

How long does a southbound crossing take?

With complete paperwork, clearance is usually same day and delivery to Monterrey takes 1 to 2 business days. Interior cities add 2 to 4 days, and a red light inspection adds 1 to 2 days.

What is the single biggest cause of delay?

A mismatch between the commercial invoice and the pedimento. It is the most common reason a southbound load is held. Verifying the documents before the freight leaves the warehouse prevents most of these delays.

Does BringGo Ship handle the handoff and clearance together?

Yes. With warehouses in Laredo and Monterrey and a licensed customs broker, the transfer and the customs release are coordinated in one place, so the trailer moves as soon as it is legally cleared.

translations.title: Türkiye'den Amazon Meksika'ya ürün nasıl gönderilir?
translations.excerpt: Türk satıcılar için Türkiye çıkışından Laredo ve Meksika FBA kabulüne kadar ürün, vergi, gümrük ve prep akışını anlatıyoruz.
translations.content:
Türkiye'den Amazon Meksika'ya ürün nasıl gönderilir?

Diyelim ki Türkiye'de üretilen küçük ev aksesuarları satıyorsunuz. İlk yükte bütün kataloğu göndermek yerine iki ürünü seçmek daha sağlıklı olur. Ürünlerin menşei nettir. Paket ölçüleri bellidir. İspanyolca etiket ihtiyacı kontrol edilir. Laredo'da sayım ve FNSKU kontrolü yapılır.

Bu küçük deneme size üç şey söyler: gerçek ithalat maliyeti, Amazon kabul süreci ve müşterinin ürüne ilgisi. Bu üçü olumluysa ikinci yükü büyütmek için elinizde tahmin değil, veri olur.

Türkiye'den Amazon Meksika'ya ürün göndermek için satış hesabından önce ithalat modelini çözmeniz gerekir. Meksika'da geçerli bir ithalatçı, RFC, doğru ürün sınıflandırması, pedimento ve ürün bazlı izinler olmadan koli FBA deposuna giremez. Türkiye ile Meksika arasında serbest ticaret anlaşması olmadığı için menşe ve vergi hesabı sevkiyattan önce yapılmalıdır.

Türkiye'den Amazon Meksika'ya nasıl gönderilir?

Pratik akış iki aşamalıdır. Ürün önce Türkiye'den ABD'ye veya doğrudan Meksika'ya taşınır; ardından Meksika ithalatı ve FBA kabulü tamamlanır. Laredo rotası, ürünleri sınırdan önce saymak, etiketlemek ve dosyayı kontrol etmek için ara durak sağlar. Bu, gümrüğü ortadan kaldırmaz. Sadece hatayı yük Meksika sınırına dayanmadan yakalamamızı sağlar.

Vergi ve gümrük hesabında en kritik nokta nedir?

Ürünün üretildiği ülke, Türkiye'den gönderildiği gerçeğinden daha önemlidir. Gümrük vergisi GTİP, menşe, gümrük değeri ve yürürlükteki önlemlere göre belirlenir. Standart Meksika IVA oranı %16'dır; ancak matrah yalnız ürün bedeli olmayabilir. Navlun, sigorta, vergi ve diğer gümrük kalemleri dosyaya göre hesaba girer. Bu nedenle internetteki tek oranla kârlılık hesabı yapmayın.

Laredo prep noktası ne kazandırır?

Türkiye'den uzun yol gelen kolilerde adet farkı, ezilme, yanlış barkod ve Amazon planıyla uyuşmayan koli ölçüsü çıkabilir. Sınırdaki prep aşaması ürünleri yeniden sayma, FNSKU kontrolü, paketleme düzeltmesi ve konsolidasyon fırsatı verir. Bizim sevmediğimiz senaryo, yanlış etiketli ürünün gümrüğü geçip FBA kabulünde reddedilmesidir; geri dönüş çok daha pahalı olur.

İlk sevkiyat neden küçük tutulmalı?

Yeni pazarda ürün uygunluğu kadar satış hızı da bilinmez. Kontrollü bir ilk parti, gümrük maliyetini, Amazon kabul farklarını, müşteri talebini ve iade nedenlerini gerçek veriden görmenizi sağlar. İlk yük sorunsuz geçti diye hemen büyük stok göndermeyin. İkinci siparişi satış ve stok dönüşü birlikte haklı çıkarsın.

Ürün sayfasını da yerelleştirin

Lojistik hazır diye satış hazır sayılmaz. Başlık, açıklama, ölçüler ve kullanım bilgileri Meksika müşterisinin anlayacağı İspanyolcayla yazılmalı. Garanti ve iade beklentisi de net olmalı. Yanlış anlaşılmış bir ürün sayfası, iyi hazırlanmış stoğu hızla iade operasyonuna çevirebilir.

Türkiye çıkışından önce hazırlanacak dosya

Her SKU için Türkçe ürün adının yanında teknik İngilizce veya İspanyolca tanım, malzeme, kullanım, üretim ülkesi, birim değer ve paket ölçüsü bulunmalı. Gümrük sınıflandırması bu bilgiler üzerinden teyit edilmeli. Amazon etiketi ile ticari fatura tanımı farklı sistemlere ait olsa da aynı fiziksel ürünü göstermeli.

İlk parti için güvenli yaklaşım

Az sayıda SKU seçin ve satış tahmininden daha küçük bir deneme stoğu gönderin. Prep merkezinden kabul, açık koli, etiket ve tamamlanmış palet fotoğrafları isteyin. Amazon teslimatından sonra kabul süresini ve fark raporunu kaydedin. İkinci parti miktarını ancak gerçek ithalat maliyeti ve satış hızı görüldüğünde büyütün.

Sık sorulan sorular

Türk şirketi kendi adına ithalat yapabilir mi?

Meksika'daki vergi ve ithalatçı kayıtları kurulmadan doğrudan ticari ithalat yapılamaz. Kendi yerel yapınız veya uygun bir kayıtlı ithalatçı modeli gerekir.

DDP gönderim tüm sorunu çözer mi?

Hayır. DDP maliyet ve sorumluluk dağılımını tanımlar; yasak ürün, eksik izin, yanlış sınıflandırma veya Amazon kabul şartlarını geçersiz kılmaz.

translations.title: Questions To Ask A Mexican Customs Broker Before Hiring One
translations.excerpt: Before hiring a Mexican customs broker, these are the questions that separate a good one from a risky one: licensing, liability, HS codes, timing and fees.
translations.content:
Before hiring a Mexican customs broker (agente aduanal), ask whether they hold a valid patente, how they handle the shared liability introduced in the 2026 reform, how they classify your HS codes, what their typical clearance time is at your crossing, how they price their service, and whether they can upload the certificate of origin digitally before shipment. The right answers protect you from delays, fines, and the wrong duty rate.

  • Under the 2026 reform, importer and broker share liability (responsabilidad solidaria) for the declaration, so the broker's diligence directly affects your risk.
  • A broker can represent a limited number of active importers per year under the 2026 rules, which affects how much attention your account gets.
  • Broker fees run roughly 3,500 to 15,000 MXN per operation, or about 0.35 to 0.65 percent of value; they are not fixed by law (camtomx).
  • In 2026 the certificate of origin must be uploaded digitally before shipment or you lose the USMCA rate (trade.gov).

What questions should I ask a Mexican customs broker?

Cover five areas: licensing and liability, HS classification, clearance timing at your crossing, transparent fees, and 2026 documentation handling. The answers reveal how much risk they take off your plate.

A good broker does more than file paperwork; they protect you from the errors that cause delays and fines. Since the 2026 reform makes the importer and broker jointly liable for the declaration, you want someone who is careful, communicative, and specific. The list below is what we would ask before signing. Treat vague answers as a warning sign: on the border, precision is the service you are paying for. BringGo Ship works with a licensed customs broker and its own warehouses in Laredo and Monterrey, so document review happens before the truck crosses, not after it is held.

The questions, one by one

Ask about the patente, liability handling, HS classification method, clearance time, fee structure, and 2026 certificate of origin process. Each maps to a real risk.

1. Do you hold a valid patente and can you share it? Only a licensed agente aduanal can file the pedimento. 2. How do you handle the 2026 shared liability, and what do you need from me to keep the declaration accurate? 3. How do you classify HS codes, and what happens if a classification is questioned? A wrong code changes duty and inspection risk. 4. What is your typical clearance time at my crossing, and how do you handle a red light (rojo)? 5. How do you price: per operation, a percentage of value, or a mix, and what is included? 6. How do you handle the certificate of origin digitally before shipment so I keep the USMCA rate? 7. How many importers do you actively represent, and who is my point of contact? 8. Can you review my documents before the freight leaves, not at the border? These eight cover the failure points that cost importers time and money.

Broker questions and the risk each one checks (2026)

QuestionRisk it checks
Valid patente?Unlicensed filing, rejected pedimento
How do you handle 2026 shared liability?Fines passed to you
HS classification method?Wrong duty, inspection risk
Typical clearance time and rojo handling?Unexpected delays
Fee structure?Hidden costs
Digital certificate of origin before shipment?Losing the USMCA rate

Update: since 1 July 2026, companies can file as well

This article describes the agente aduanal, the licensed individual who holds a personal patente. That is still valid and still the most common arrangement. It is no longer the only one.

Since 1 July 2026 Mexico allows authorized legal entities, called agencias aduanales, to promote customs clearance across all 50 customs offices, under every regime in the Customs Law. The scheme opened nationally after a pilot that ran from 19 May to 30 June 2026, coordinated by ANAM, SAT and the Ministry of Economy, which defines the figure in one sentence:

“La agencia aduanal es la persona moral autorizada para promover el despacho aduanero de mercancías bajo los distintos regímenes aduaneros, de conformidad con lo establecido en la Ley Aduanera.”

Secretaría de Economía

For an importer the practical difference is continuity and accountability. An authorization held by a company survives one person's absence, illness or suspension, and it gives you a counterparty you can contract with and audit. Both structures are valid, so the question to ask a provider is simply which one they operate under.

One more change from the same reform matters more than the structure: importers and brokers are now jointly responsible for the accuracy of customs data, tariff classification, valuation and duty payment. The classification and value questions raised in this article are no longer only your broker's problem.

Definitions

  • Patente: The patente is the license number that authorizes an agente aduanal to file customs declarations in Mexico.
  • Responsabilidad solidaria: Responsabilidad solidaria is the 2026 rule under which importer and broker share liability for the customs declaration.

Frequently asked questions

Do I legally need a customs broker in Mexico?

For commercial imports, yes: only a registered agente aduanal can file the pedimento. The 2026 reform kept this requirement and added shared liability, which makes choosing a careful broker more important, not less.

How much should a customs broker cost?

Roughly 3,500 to 15,000 MXN per operation, or about 0.35 to 0.65 percent of the goods value. Fees are not fixed by law, so ask exactly what is included and whether classification and document review are part of the price.

What is the biggest red flag in a broker's answers?

Vagueness about HS classification and liability. If they cannot explain how they classify your goods or how they handle the 2026 shared liability, they are shifting risk to you. Precision is the service you are paying for.

Can a broker help me keep the USMCA duty rate?

Yes, if they upload the certificate of origin digitally before the shipment, as 2026 rules require. Ask them to confirm this step in writing; missing it means paying the full third country duty instead of the preferential rate.

Should the broker review documents before shipping?

Absolutely. The cheapest way to avoid a held load is to verify the invoice, HS codes, and certificate of origin while the freight is still at the warehouse. A good broker offers this as standard, not as an extra.

translations.title: Amazon Remote Fulfillment Mı, Yerel Meksika Deposu Mu?
translations.excerpt: NARF ile ABD FBA stoğunuzdan Meksika'ya satarsınız; yerel depoda stok Meksika'da durur. Hangisi size uygun: süre, maliyet ve vergi farkını netleştiriyoruz.
translations.content:
NARF (Amazon Remote Fulfillment), ABD'deki FBA stoğunuzdan Meksika'daki müşteriye satış yapmanızı sağlar; ayrı stok tutmazsınız ama teslimat uzar ve ithalat vergisini müşteri öder. Yerel Meksika deposunda ise stok ülke içinde durur: teslimat hızlıdır ve deneyim daha iyidir, karşılığında stoğu önden Meksika'ya taşımanız gerekir. Kısa cevap: test ve düşük hacim için NARF, düzenli ve yüksek hacim için yerel depo mantıklıdır.

  • NARF'ta ithalat vergisini ve gümrüğü kayıtlı ithalatçı (IOR) sıfatıyla müşteri öder; bu, iade ve deneyimi zorlaştırabilir (sell.amazon.com).
  • NARF teslimat süresi yerel FBA'e göre daha uzundur çünkü her sipariş sınırı geçer.
  • Yerel depoda stok Meksika'da olduğu için Laredo aktarmalı modelde teslimat büyük şehirlerde genellikle 1 ile 3 iş günüdür.
  • Yerel ithalatta ABD menşeli mal T-MEC kapsamında çoğu üründe yüzde 0 gümrük vergisine tabidir; üstüne yüzde 16 IVA gelir.

NARF ile mi yerel depoyla mı satmalı?

Hacminize bağlı. Düşük hacimde ve pazarı test ederken NARF hızlı başlangıçtır. Düzenli ve yüksek hacimde yerel depo hem teslimatı hızlandırır hem müşteri deneyimini iyileştirir.

NARF, ABD'deki mevcut FBA stoğunuzu Meksika müşterisine açar. Avantajı, ayrı stok yatırımı yapmadan yeni bir pazarı denemektir. Bedeli ise iki yerde ödenir: her sipariş tek tek sınırı geçtiği için teslimat uzar, ve ithalat vergisi kayıtlı ithalatçı sıfatıyla müşteriye yansıtılır. Bu, sepet terkini ve iade sürtünmesini artırabilir. Yerel Meksika deposu ise stoğu ülke içine alır; müşteri siparişi verdiğinde mal zaten Meksika'dadır, dolayısıyla teslimat hızlı ve öngörülebilir olur. Karşılığında stoğu önden toplu biçimde Meksika'ya taşımanız ve yerel ithalat sürecini yönetmeniz gerekir. BringGo Ship'in çift ülke deposu ve lisanslı gümrük müşaviri, bu yerel modelde stoğu Laredo üzerinden Meksika'ya geçirip Monterrey deposundan dağıtmayı tek elden mümkün kılar. Aşağıdaki tablo iki modeli aynı ölçütlerle karşılaştırır.

Maliyet ve vergi farkı nedir?

NARF'ta vergiyi müşteri öder ve teslimat maliyeti sipariş başına yüksektir. Yerel depoda vergiyi baştan siz çözersiniz ve toplu ithalat kilogram maliyetini düşürür.

NARF modelinde ürün ABD'de kaldığı için stok yatırımınız düşüktür, ancak her siparişte sınır geçişi ve müşteriye yansıyan ithalat vergisi vardır; bu da fiyat rekabetinde ve deneyimde dezavantaj yaratır. Yerel depo modelinde stoğu toplu olarak ithal edersiniz: ABD menşeli mallar T-MEC kapsamında çoğu üründe yüzde 0 gümrük vergisine tabidir, üstüne yüzde 16 IVA eklenir. Toplu sevkiyat kilogram başına maliyeti düşürdüğü için, düzenli satışta yerel model genellikle daha ekonomiktir. Karar için basit bir ölçüt: aylık sipariş adediniz istikrarlıysa ve teslimat hızı satışınızı etkiliyorsa yerel depo; henüz talebi ölçüyorsanız NARF ile başlayıp hacim oturunca yerele geçmek mantıklıdır.

Tanımlar

  • NARF: NARF, Amazon'un ABD'deki FBA stoğundan Meksika müşterisine satış yapmanızı sağlayan uzaktan gönderim modelidir.
  • IOR: IOR (kayıtlı ithalatçı), ithalatın yasal sorumluluğunu kendi adına üstlenen taraftır; NARF'ta bu genellikle müşteridir.

Sık sorulan sorular

NARF için Meksika'da şirket gerekir mi?

Hayır, NARF'ta stok ABD'de kalır ve ithalatı sipariş bazında müşteri kayıtlı ithalatçı sıfatıyla üstlenir. Yerel depo modelinde ise ticari ithalat için RFC ve ithalatçı kaydı ya da bir IOR partneri gerekir.

Hangisi daha hızlı teslim eder?

Yerel depo. Stok Meksika'da olduğu için teslimat büyük şehirlerde genellikle 1 ile 3 iş günüdür. NARF'ta her sipariş sınırı tek tek geçtiği için süre daha uzundur ve müşteri deneyimini etkiler.

Düşük hacimle başlıyorum, hangisi?

NARF. Ayrı stok yatırımı yapmadan pazarı test edersiniz. Satış istikrar kazanıp teslimat hızı rekabet unsuru olduğunda yerel Meksika deposuna geçmek maliyeti düşürür ve deneyimi iyileştirir.

Yerel depoya geçince gümrük nasıl işler?

Stoğu toplu ithal edersiniz: lisanslı müşavir pedimentoyu hazırlar, ABD menşeli mallar çoğu üründe yüzde 0 gümrük vergisine tabidir, üstüne yüzde 16 IVA gelir. BringGo Ship bu geçişi Laredo ve Monterrey depolarıyla tek elden yürütür.

translations.title: What is a pedimento and how do you read one?
translations.excerpt: A plain-English guide to the Mexican pedimento, the fields importers should review, and the supporting documents behind the declaration.
translations.content:
What is a pedimento and how do you read one?

Why was this tariff code selected? What evidence supports the country of origin? How was the customs value built? An importer who can answer those three questions understands the core of the entry.

You do not need to memorize every pedimento key. You do need to recognize your company, your products, and the commercial facts. If a line looks unfamiliar, ask before transmission. The most useful broker relationship is not silent. It leaves the importer with a clear record of what was declared and why.

A pedimento is Mexico's electronic customs declaration for commercial imports and exports. It identifies the parties, merchandise, tariff classification, origin, customs value, regime, duties, and supporting records. An authorized customs professional prepares and transmits it, but the importer should still review the business facts. Treating it as a receipt with one amount at the bottom misses the fields that create future audit risk.

What is a pedimento and who prepares it?

The importer provides product, transaction, and registration information to the customs broker. The broker translates that file into the official declaration, attaches or references required digital documents, calculates charges, and transmits the entry through Mexico's customs system. The commercial invoice, bill of lading, origin evidence, permits, and value documents support the filing. They do not become interchangeable simply because they describe the same shipment.

  • Importer and RFC: Legal party responsible · Importer records
  • Tariff code: Classification and controls · Product specifications
  • Origin and export country: Where made and routed · Origin evidence
  • Customs value: Declared valuation basis · Invoice and payment
  • Regime and keys: Legal customs treatment · Commercial purpose
  • Contributions: Duty, IVA, and other charges · Broker calculation

Which mistakes matter most?

Country of shipment is often confused with country of origin. Goods shipped from a US warehouse are not automatically USMCA-origin goods. Product descriptions can also be too vague to support the selected code. Finally, value, currency, Incoterm, and payment evidence may conflict. Mexico's 2026 electronic value controls make those inconsistencies more visible before entry, so the commercial team and broker must use the same facts.

How should an importer review the document?

Compare legal name and RFC first. Then match each line to the invoice, quantities, weights, description, tariff code, origin, and value. Ask why a preference, permit, or tax treatment applies. Keep the final declaration and supporting evidence with the shipment record. We prefer a short pre-filing review for new products. Ten minutes before transmission is cheaper than a correction after release.

Keep a product master sheet

For repeat SKUs, store the approved description, material, use, origin, tariff code, unit value logic, and required permits. Give the broker controlled updates when the product changes. This reduces accidental drift between shipments. It also makes internal review much faster when a buyer or auditor asks what was declared.

Review it in three passes

  1. Match the importer, supplier, invoice, regime, and customs office to the shipment.
  2. Match each product line to quantity, unit, origin, tariff classification, and declared value.
  3. Review duties, VAT, fees, preferences, permits, and attached electronic records.

Do not approve a line because the total looks familiar. A repeated SKU can still carry a changed origin, value, or specification. Keep the approved version with the invoice, payment evidence, classification note, and release record. If a correction is required, preserve both versions and the reason for the change.

The obligation is written into the Customs Law itself, and it is worth reading in the original because it defines both what a pedimento is and how it must be filed:

“Quienes introduzcan o extraigan mercancías del territorio nacional destinándolas a un régimen aduanero, están obligados a transmitir a las autoridades aduaneras, a través del sistema electrónico aduanero, en documento electrónico, un pedimento con información referente a las citadas mercancías.”

Ley Aduanera, Article 36 (Mexico)

Frequently asked questions

Is a pedimento the same as a commercial invoice?

No. The invoice records the transaction. The pedimento is the customs declaration supported by that invoice and other evidence.

Can an importer correct a pedimento?

Corrections may be possible depending on the field and timing, but they can create cost and scrutiny. Prevent the error before filing whenever possible.

translations.title: FTL transit time from Laredo to Monterrey
translations.excerpt: A realistic FTL timeline for the Laredo to Monterrey corridor, including customs, transfer, inland dispatch, and the risks behind delays.
translations.content:
FTL transit time from Laredo to Monterrey

Imagine a load ready at noon in Laredo. The entry file is complete, duty funding is available, and the receiver has an open appointment. That load has a good chance of moving smoothly. Change one fact and the schedule changes. A missing value document can consume the afternoon. A late release can miss the receiver window.

This is why our timeline has checkpoints instead of one promise. The shipper sees what is ready, what is waiting, and who owns the next action.

A properly prepared FTL load can often move from Laredo to Monterrey in 1 · 2 business days. That estimate includes the border process. The road drive is only one part of the timeline. A customs inspection, late arrival, missing value evidence, driver handoff, or delivery appointment can add time. We never sell the roughly three-hour road distance as a three-hour cross-border service.

What is the FTL transit time from Laredo to Monterrey?

For planning, separate warehouse release, export processing, Mexican import clearance, border transfer, and inland delivery. When the pedimento file and funds are ready before the truck arrives, these stages can connect quickly. When the broker first sees the documents at arrival, the load may sit even though the tractor is available. Friday afternoon arrivals deserve their own plan because customs and receiver schedules may not align through the weekend.

Why can two identical routes have different transit times?

The shipment profile changes the customs risk. A known SKU with a validated classification and complete importer file is different from a mixed load with new products. The receiver also matters. A flexible warehouse can unload when the truck arrives; a plant or marketplace appointment may require a fixed window. Weather, bridge traffic, inspections, and carrier capacity add variables that no mileage calculator can see.

What should an FTL quote include?

Ask whether the quote includes Laredo handling, transfer carrier, cross-border movement, Mexico line haul, waiting time, tolls, appointment delivery, and return of equipment. Customs brokerage, duties, IVA, inspections, and storage should be clearly separated. A low line-haul rate with undefined border charges is not a complete quote. Also confirm whether the freight remains in one trailer or is cross-docked.

SegmentOperational taskMain variable
Laredo warehouseCount, seal, and releaseCargo discrepancy
Customs filePedimento and supporting documentsClassification or value
Border transferCarrier and tractor handoffQueue and equipment
Mexico dispatchCarta Porte and route releaseData mismatch
Monterrey deliveryReceiver appointmentWindow and unloading

Share one operating timeline

The shipper, broker, warehouse, and carrier should see the same target times. Mark which times are confirmed and which are estimates. If customs releases late, update the receiver before the truck departs. A realistic revised appointment is better than a driver waiting outside a closed dock.

Plan the clock from the receiver backward

Start with the delivery appointment. Allow time for Mexican line haul, release, presentation, transfer, and warehouse checkout. Then set the latest acceptable arrival in Laredo. This backward plan exposes late paperwork before the truck is booked.

When the plan changes

Do not keep the original delivery estimate after a missed cutoff. Confirm the new customs window, driver availability, and receiver slot. Share one revised time with every party. FTL reduces consolidation stops, but it does not remove customs, transfer, hours of service, traffic, or a closed receiving dock.

Frequently asked questions

Can Laredo to Monterrey deliver the same day?

It can happen with early release and aligned operations, but it should not be promised as a universal service. Border and receiver conditions control the result.

Does FTL avoid customs inspection?

No. FTL reduces consolidation and handling, not customs authority. The shipment remains subject to document and physical controls.

translations.title: Meksika için Amazon FBA prep center nasıl seçilir?
translations.excerpt: Sınırdaki bir prep center'ın etiket, koli, sayım, gümrük ve FBA teslimatında hangi kontrolleri gerçekten yapması gerektiğini anlatıyoruz.
translations.content:
Meksika için Amazon FBA prep center nasıl seçilir?

Ürünün üstünde bir etiket olması yeterli değildir. Etiket doğru SKU'ya ait olmalı. Koli içeriği sevkiyat planıyla eşleşmeli. Ürün güvenli paketlenmeli. Sayım farkı varsa müşteri bilgilendirilmeli. Bunların hepsi kayıt altına alınmalı.

Ben ilk partide fotoğraf istemeyi faydalı buluyorum. Her üründen bir örnek, bir açık koli ve tamamlanmış palet fotoğrafı yeter. Böylece hem talimatın doğru anlaşıldığını görürsünüz hem de sonraki partiler için referans oluşur.

İyi bir Meksika FBA prep center yalnız etiket yapıştırmaz. Ürünü sayar, hasarı kaydeder, Amazon sevkiyat planıyla koli içeriğini eşleştirir, FNSKU ve görünür barkodları kontrol eder, gümrük dosyasındaki ürün tanımıyla fiziksel ürünü karşılaştırır. Sınırda bulunmasının değeri, hatayı Meksika ithalatından ve Amazon kabulünden önce yakalamasıdır.

Meksika FBA prep hizmetini kim yapıyor?

Hizmeti seçerken depo adresinden çok süreç sahipliğine bakın. Sadece ABD içi Amazon hazırlığı yapan bir depo, Meksika ithalatındaki RFC, pedimento, menşe ve ürün izinlerini takip etmeyebilir. Sadece gümrük yapan bir ekip de Amazon koli kurallarını bilmeyebilir. Laredo'da iki tarafı birlikte yöneten model, prep çıktısını gümrük ve son teslim planına bağlar.

FNSKU kontrolünde neye dikkat edilir?

Her birimin taranabilir ve doğru ürünle eşleşen barkodu olmalıdır. Seller Central hangi barkod türünü bekliyorsa prep buna göre yapılır. Yanlış etiketi doğru ürünün üstüne düzgün yapıştırmak yine hatadır. Ürün adı, kondisyon, adet ve sevkiyat planı çapraz kontrol edilmelidir. Barkodun katlanmaması, kapatılmaması ve başka görünür kodlarla tarayıcıyı şaşırtmaması gerekir.

Prep fiyat teklifinde hangi kalemler görünmeli?

Kabul, sayım, etiket, poşetleme, balonlu koruma, koli, paletleme, depolama, fotoğraf, imha, iade ve çıkış ücretlerini ayrı isteyin. Minimum işlem bedeli ve malzeme fiyatı da yazılı olsun. Aceleniz yoksa her işi ekspres yapmak gereksizdir. Fakat Amazon randevusuna yetişecek yük için iş emri önceliği ve günlük kapasite önceden konuşulmalıdır.

İlk iş emrinde nasıl test yapılır?

Tek bir SKU'dan örnek birim hazırlatın ve fotoğrafla onaylayın. Ardından küçük partide tarama, sayım ve koli içeriği raporunu karşılaştırın. Hata varsa tüm envantere uygulamadan talimatı düzeltin. Prep center'ın kalite sürecini gerçek ürün üzerinde görmek, sunumdaki hizmet listesinden daha güvenilir bir seçim ölçütüdür. Onaylı örneği sonraki partiler için yazılı referans olarak saklayın.

  • Kabul: Adet ve hasar kaydı · Fotoğraf ve sayım raporu
  • Ürün etiketi: Beklenen barkodu doğrulama · Örnek etiket görüntüsü
  • Paketleme: Ürün tipine uygun koruma · Düzeltme ve malzeme kaydı
  • Koli planı: Seller Central planıyla eşleme · Koli içerik listesi
  • Sınır teslimi: Gümrük ve taşıma koordinasyonu · Takip ve teslim kanıtı

Hata raporu isteyin

Prep center yalnız tamamlanan adetleri değil, bulunan sorunları da bildirmeli. Yanlış etiket, hasarlı ambalaj, eksik ürün ve koli farkı ayrı görünmeli. Aynı hata tekrar ediyorsa tedarikçi talimatını düzeltin. Prep hizmetinin değeri sadece düzeltmek değil, hatanın kaynağını göstermektir.

Prep merkezine gönderilecek kısa talimat

SKU listesi, beklenen adet, barkod türü, paketleme kuralı, koli sınırı, son teslim tarihi ve hata durumunda aranacak kişi tek belgede bulunmalı. Ürün üzerinde eski barkodlar görünüyorsa ne yapılacağı yazılmalı. Koli içeriği ile Seller Central planı aynı referansı kullanmalı.

Kabul raporunda görmek istediklerimiz

  • Beklenen, gelen ve hazırlanan adet
  • Hasarlı veya eksik ürün fotoğrafı
  • Etiket ve paketleme hatası sayısı
  • Koli ölçüsü, ağırlığı ve içeriği
  • Palet fotoğrafı ve çıkış zamanı

Bu rapor yalnız kontrol için değil, tedarikçiyi geliştirmek için de kullanılır.

Prep noktasının yeri neden önemli?

Prep işlemi iki yerde yapılabilir: yükün çıkış ülkesinde ya da sınırın ABD tarafında, geçişten hemen önce. İkisi aynı iş gibi görünür; fark, hata anında ortaya çıkar.

Çıkış ülkesinde yapılan prep, yolda bir şey değişirse düzeltme şansı bırakmaz. Etiket standardı güncellenmişse, koli içeriği planla uyuşmuyorsa ya da ürünün bir kısmı yolda hasar görmüşse, sorun ancak Amazon deposunda ortaya çıkar. Oradaki düzeltme ise en pahalı düzeltmedir.

Sınırın ABD tarafındaki bir prep noktası, ürünü geçişten önce son kez görme imkânı verir. Eksik etiket burada tamamlanır, hasarlı ürün burada ayrılır, sayım farkı burada kayda geçer. Amazon'a giden koli, kontrolden geçmiş koli olur.

Laredo'daki depomuzda bu kontrolü geçiş öncesinde biz yapıyoruz. Böylece FBA randevusuna giden yükün içinde sürpriz kalmıyor.

translations.title: How US To Mexico Cross-Border Shipping Works: The Complete Guide
translations.excerpt: Cross-border shipping to Mexico follows a clear sequence: export, border transfer, customs clearance and delivery. This guide walks through every step, with real times and costs.
translations.content:
Cross-border shipping from the US to Mexico works in five steps: your goods leave a US warehouse, US export is completed, a transfer tractor moves the trailer across the border, a licensed broker files the pedimento and pays duty and IVA, and the goods are released for delivery. With complete paperwork, clearance at Laredo is usually same day and delivery to Monterrey takes 1 to 2 business days. Commercial imports require a Mexican RFC and a customs broker.

  • A licensed customs broker (agente aduanal) must file the pedimento; since January 2025 every import declaration requires the importer of record's RFC (trade.gov).
  • Import IVA is 16 percent (SAT, trade.gov).
  • US origin goods enter at 0 percent duty on most products under the USMCA; goods from countries without a treaty face higher tariffs under the 2026 decree.
  • A well documented full truckload from Laredo reaches Monterrey in 1 to 2 business days (BringGo Ship operations data).
  • Laredo is North America's busiest inland port, with more than 17,000 trucks crossing per day (City of Laredo, 2026).

How does cross-border shipping from the US to Mexico work?

It is a chain of five steps that connects a US warehouse to a Mexican destination: export from the US, transfer across the border, customs clearance in Mexico, release, and domestic delivery.

Cross-border shipping is not one movement but a coordinated sequence. Your goods leave a US warehouse, ideally after the documents have been checked. US export formalities are completed on the American side. A transfer tractor then moves the trailer to the Mexican side of the border, a short step known as transfer or drayage. There, a licensed customs broker files the pedimento, the official import declaration, and pays the duty and IVA. Mexican customs assigns a green or red light, and once the goods are released, a domestic carrier takes them to their destination, such as Monterrey. Most of this traffic runs through Laredo because it is North America's busiest inland port. An operator with warehouses on both sides of the border can run the whole chain from one place: BringGo Ship works this model from its Laredo and Monterrey warehouses with a licensed customs broker.

What are the steps, from the US warehouse to a Mexican doorstep?

Five: leave the US warehouse, complete US export, transfer across the border, clear the pedimento in Mexico, and deliver domestically.

Seeing the shipment as steps makes it clear where a load can stall. First, the goods leave the US warehouse; this is the moment to confirm the invoice, packing list, and classifications. Second, US export formalities are completed on the American side. Third, the transfer or drayage tractor physically moves the trailer into Mexico. Fourth, the customs broker transmits and clears the pedimento, paying duty and IVA; at this point customs decides the light. Fifth, the released goods move by domestic transport to their final destination. Each step depends on the one before it, so an incomplete document in step one becomes a delay in step four. That is why a document review before the freight leaves the warehouse is the best use of time in the entire process.

What documents do you need to ship to Mexico?

Five core documents: commercial invoice, packing list, correct HS codes, certificate of origin for the USMCA rate, and the Complemento Carta Porte for the Mexican road leg.

The shipment rests on a consistent set of documents. The commercial invoice sets the value and description; the packing list details the contents per pallet with weights and dimensions; the HS codes (tariff classification) determine the duty and must be correct, because a wrong code raises inspection risk. The certificate of origin is what earns the USMCA preferential rate, and in 2026 it must be uploaded digitally before the shipment; if it is missing, you pay the full third country duty. The Complemento Carta Porte is required for road transport inside Mexico. The rule that prevents most delays is simple: the invoice, packing list, and pedimento must say exactly the same thing in value, quantity, and description.

How long does cross-border shipping to Mexico take?

With complete paperwork, clearance is usually same day and delivery to Monterrey takes 1 to 2 business days. Interior points add 2 to 4 days, and a red light adds 1 to 2 days.

Transit time is driven by customs, not distance. The Laredo infrastructure is fast because of its volume, so documentation is what makes the difference. With complete, consistent papers, clearance is usually same day and the goods reach Monterrey in 1 to 2 business days. For interior destinations like Mexico City, add 2 to 4 days of domestic transport. If the load draws a red light (rojo), physical inspection adds 1 to 2 days. Season matters too: around El Buen Fin in November and the December peak, the bridge and customs get busier, so leave a 2 to 3 day buffer. The table below summarizes the southbound timeline through Laredo.

How much does it cost to ship to Mexico?

The fiscal cost combines the broker fee, duty, and IVA, plus freight. IVA is 16 percent; duty is 0 percent on most US origin goods under the USMCA.

The landed cost of a shipment has a few parts. The customs broker fee runs roughly 3,500 to 15,000 MXN per operation, or about 0.35 to 0.65 percent of value. Import IVA is 16 percent. Duty depends on origin: US origin goods enter at 0 percent on most products under the USMCA. A 2026 point to note: the decree effective January 1 raised tariffs to between 10 and 50 percent on about 1,648 tariff lines (1,463 plus 185 added in April 2026) for goods from countries without a treaty, such as China. There is also a de minimis for US origin goods under the USMCA: no tax up to 50 US dollars and no duty up to 117 US dollars. On top of the fiscal cost sits the freight itself. Because rates and rules shift, confirm the tariff for your product with your broker before each season.

Do you need a Mexican RFC and a customs broker?

For commercial imports, yes to both. Only a licensed broker can file the pedimento, and an RFC is required; if you lack one, an importer of record (IOR) lets you start.

Two requirements are non-negotiable for commercial importing. First, an RFC (the Mexican tax ID) and importer registration; since January 2025 every import declaration requires the importer of record's RFC, and the courier channel now asks for the consignee RFC as well. Second, a licensed customs broker (agente aduanal), because only a registered broker can file the pedimento. The 2026 reform added shared liability, so the importer and broker are jointly responsible for the declaration. If you do not yet have your own RFC, you can still ship through a partner that acts as the importer of record and clears the goods in its name while you complete your registration. This is a common way for a new seller to start selling into Mexico without waiting on paperwork.

Should you use LTL or FTL?

Roughly up to six pallets, less than truckload (LTL) is cheaper; for a full trailer, full truckload (FTL) is faster and clears on a single pedimento.

The choice comes down to volume. FTL means the trailer is yours: it moves on your schedule, crosses on a single pedimento, and is handled less, so there is less risk of damage or delay. For Laredo to Monterrey, a well documented FTL load usually arrives in 1 to 2 business days. LTL suits smaller volumes, roughly one to six pallets, where your freight shares the trailer with other shipments; that lowers the cost per pallet but adds consolidation time. A practical threshold: up to about six pallets, LTL is usually economical; a full trailer or an urgent, fragile load points to FTL. As your volume grows, moving to FTL tends to lower your per unit cost and speed up the border, so it is worth reviewing the mix regularly.

What are the most common mistakes that delay a shipment?

An invoice that does not match the pedimento, a wrong HS code, and a missing or late certificate of origin. All three are preventable before departure.

Most delays come from avoidable errors at the origin. The most common is an inconsistency between the invoice and the pedimento in value, quantity, or description, which triggers a hold. Next is an incorrect HS code, which changes the duty and raises the chance of a red light. Third, increasingly relevant in 2026, is failing to upload the certificate of origin digitally before shipment, which costs you the USMCA rate. Timing adds risk too: a trailer that reaches the border late on a Friday can sit through the weekend. Under the 2026 reform, the importer and broker share liability, so accuracy matters more than ever. The fix is always the same: verify every document while the freight is still at the warehouse, not at the bridge.

Ley Aduanera, Article 35 (Mexico)

  • Pedimento: The pedimento is Mexico's official electronic import declaration, filed by a licensed customs broker.
  • Transfer or drayage: The transfer is the short move that hands the trailer from one side of the border to the other during clearance.
  • IVA: IVA is Mexico's value added tax, with a standard rate of 16 percent.
  • RFC: The RFC is the Mexican tax ID required to import goods commercially.

Your goods leave a US warehouse, clear US export, a transfer tractor moves them across the border, a licensed broker clears the pedimento and pays duty and IVA, and a domestic carrier delivers them. With good paperwork, Laredo to Monterrey takes 1 to 2 business days.

Do I need a customs broker to ship to Mexico?

For commercial imports, yes. Only a registered agente aduanal can file the pedimento. You provide the invoice and product details; the broker classifies the goods, calculates duty and IVA, and transmits the declaration to the SAT.

Do I need a Mexican RFC?

Yes for commercial imports. Since January 2025 every import declaration requires the importer of record's RFC. If you do not have one, you can ship through a partner acting as importer of record while you complete your own registration.

How long does it take to ship from the US to Mexico?

With complete paperwork, clearance is usually same day and delivery to Monterrey takes 1 to 2 business days. Interior cities like Mexico City add 2 to 4 days, and a red light inspection adds 1 to 2 days.

US origin goods enter at 0 percent on most products under the USMCA, plus 16 percent IVA. In 2026, goods from countries without a treaty can pay 5 to 50 percent on about 1,648 tariff lines (1,463 plus 185 added in April 2026). Confirm your product's tariff with your broker.

LTL shares the trailer with other shipments and suits about one to six pallets, lowering cost per pallet but adding days. FTL is a dedicated trailer, faster and cleaner at the border, and better for full or urgent loads.

The pedimento is the legal heart of every Mexican import. It is an electronic declaration that records the value, the classification, the origin, the duty, the IVA, and the parties to the transaction. Nothing crosses into the Mexican market without one for a commercial shipment. By law it must be filed by an agente aduanal, a customs broker licensed by the authorities; a company cannot self file the way an experienced US importer sometimes can at home. The broker takes your commercial documents, assigns the tariff classification, calculates what is owed, pays it, and transmits the declaration. Because the pedimento must agree with the invoice and the packing list down to the value and the quantity, the broker is also your last line of defense against an error that would trigger an inspection. Mexican customs uses a light mechanism to decide which shipments to inspect. When the broker pays the pedimento, the system evaluates the declaration and returns a result: green means release, red means inspection. A green light lets the goods leave the customs area immediately, which is why a clean shipment can clear the same day. Selection is partly random and partly risk based, so a history of accurate declarations, correct classifications, and consistent documents lowers your exposure over time. You cannot control a random check, but you can control everything that raises risk: a wrong HS code, a value that does not match the invoice, or a missing certificate of origin. Reduce those, and most of your shipments run green.

How long does customs clearance take at the Mexico border?

With complete, consistent documents, a green light clears the same day at Laredo. A red light adds one to two days for physical inspection, and peak seasons add buffer time.

Clearance time is driven by documents and the light, not by distance. When the paperwork is complete and consistent and the shipment draws a green light, clearance at Laredo is usually done the same day, and the goods reach Monterrey in one to two business days. Get that right and the border is rarely the bottleneck.

Two charges make up the fiscal cost at the border. The first is IVA, Mexico's value added tax, at a standard 16 percent for qualifying operations. The 2026 reform tightened responsibility across the board. The change with the widest reach is joint liability: the importer and the customs broker are now jointly responsible for the accuracy of the declaration, so an error is no longer only the broker's problem. Documentation moved earlier in the process too; the certificate of origin has to be uploaded digitally before the shipment departs, which means origin planning now happens before the truck loads, not at the border. The honest answer is that the cost splits into two layers, and only one of them is fixed. The fiscal layer is set by rule: a customs broker fee of roughly 3,500 to 15,000 MXN per operation, the 16 percent import IVA, any duty, and small statutory fees such as the DTA and prevalidation. These you can estimate in advance because they follow the value and the classification of the goods. The second layer is the freight, and it is genuinely variable, driven by whether you move less than a truckload or a full trailer, by the lane, by fuel, and by season. Anyone who quotes you a single flat number for shipping to Mexico is guessing at the freight or hiding the fiscal detail. The useful way to budget is to calculate the fiscal cost precisely from your value and HS code, then request a current freight quote for your specific lane and volume. That gives you a real landed cost rather than a rule of thumb.

What makes up the landed cost of a Mexico shipment?

Five parts: the customs broker fee, the import duty, the 16 percent IVA, the small customs fees (DTA and prevalidation), and the freight. Origin decides the duty; volume decides most of the freight.

Landed cost is simply the sum of everything it takes to get your goods delivered and legally cleared in Mexico. First is the customs broker fee, roughly 3,500 to 15,000 MXN per operation or about 0.35 to 0.65 percent of value, which pays for classification and the pedimento. Second is the import duty, which is 0 percent for most US origin goods under the USMCA but can be much higher for non treaty origin. Third is the IVA at 16 percent, calculated on the value plus duty and certain charges. Fourth are the small statutory customs fees, mainly the DTA and the electronic prevalidation, each modest but always present. Fifth is the freight, the physical transport, which is usually the largest single line for a typical shipment. Getting landed cost right means adding all five, not just comparing freight quotes. Two carriers with the same freight rate can leave you with very different totals if one manages the fiscal side well and the other does not.

How much does a customs broker cost in Mexico?

A licensed broker typically charges 3,500 to 15,000 MXN per operation, or about 0.35 to 0.65 percent of the shipment value. The fee covers classification, the pedimento, and payment of duty and IVA.

A licensed customs broker, the agente aduanal, is not optional for a commercial import, so its fee is a fixed part of the budget. The range in practice is roughly 3,500 to 15,000 MXN per operation, or about 0.35 to 0.65 percent of the value of the goods, with the exact figure depending on the complexity of the shipment, the number of tariff lines, and the value. That fee covers real work: classifying each product with its HS code, preparing and transmitting the pedimento, and paying the duty and IVA to the SAT on your behalf. Under the 2026 reform the broker also shares liability with you for the accuracy of the declaration, which is part of what you are paying for. It is worth comparing brokers on service and accuracy rather than on price alone, because a cheap broker who triggers a red light or a reclassification can cost you far more in delay than the fee it saved. An operator that keeps the document work under one roof, like BringGo Ship at Laredo, folds this into a single coordinated service.

How much duty and IVA will you pay?

IVA is 16 percent. Duty is 0 percent on most US origin goods under the USMCA, but non treaty origin can pay 5 to 50 percent under the 2026 decree.

These two charges usually decide whether a Mexico shipment is cheap or expensive to import. IVA is straightforward at 16 percent for qualifying operations; it is calculated on the customs value plus the duty and certain charges. Duty is where origin does the heavy lifting. Under the USMCA, most US origin goods enter at 0 percent duty, which is the single biggest reason to source or consolidate in the US before crossing. Goods from countries without a treaty face a very different bill: the decree effective January 1, 2026 raised tariffs to between 10 and 50 percent on about 1,648 tariff lines total, after an April 2026 decree added 185 to the original 1,463, targeting origins such as China, and it runs through December 31, 2026. For small shipments of US origin goods there is relief through the de minimis: no tax up to 50 US dollars and no duty up to 117 US dollars. Because a wrong classification can move you into a higher duty band, confirm your HS code and origin with the broker before you ship.

What are the customs fees: DTA and prevalidation?

The DTA is a customs processing fee, a fixed amount of about 362 MXN per pedimento for USMCA operations or 0.8 percent of value in general. Electronic prevalidation adds about 238 MXN per operation.

Beyond the broker fee, duty, and IVA, two smaller statutory charges appear on almost every import and are easy to overlook. The first is the DTA, the customs processing fee set by the Ley Federal de Derechos. For general definitive imports it is 0.8 percent of the customs value, but for operations under a treaty such as the USMCA it is a fixed amount, about 362 MXN per pedimento in 2026, and it is updated quarterly for inflation. That fixed treaty rate is another quiet advantage of shipping US origin goods. The second charge is the electronic prevalidation of the pedimento, mandatory and paid to an authorized provider, at roughly 238 MXN per operation. Neither fee is large on its own, but they are real and predictable, so include them when you build a landed cost. Leaving them out is a common reason a first estimate comes in lower than the final invoice.

How much does the freight itself cost (LTL vs FTL)?

Freight is the variable part and depends on volume, lane, and season, so it is quoted, not fixed. Less than truckload suits about one to six pallets; a full truckload is priced per trailer.

Freight is the layer that resists a single number, because it moves with volume, lane, fuel, and season. Rather than quote a figure that would be out of date next quarter, it is more useful to understand the two modes and when each is economical. Less than truckload (LTL) means your pallets share a trailer with other shipments; you pay for the space you use, which is efficient for roughly one to six pallets but adds consolidation time. Full truckload (FTL) means the trailer is yours; it is priced per trailer, moves on your schedule, crosses on a single pedimento, and is handled less. As a rough guide, up to about six pallets LTL is usually the cheaper choice, while a full or urgent load points to FTL, and Laredo to Monterrey on a well documented FTL is typically one to two business days. Because rates change, the right move is to get a current quote for your exact lane and volume and pair it with the fiscal cost above to see the true landed cost.

How can you lower your cost to ship to Mexico?

Ship US origin goods to claim the 0 percent USMCA duty and the fixed DTA, consolidate to fill trailers, classify correctly to avoid reclassification, and get documents right to avoid red light delays.

Most savings come from structure, not from haggling over freight. The largest lever is origin: US origin goods qualify for 0 percent duty under the USMCA and the fixed treaty DTA, so sourcing or consolidating in the US before crossing can cut the fiscal cost dramatically compared with non treaty origin now facing the 2026 tariffs. The second lever is volume: consolidating smaller orders into fuller trailers lowers the freight per unit and reduces the number of pedimentos and broker fees you pay. The third is accuracy: a correct HS code the first time avoids reclassification and the delay that follows, and consistent documents keep you out of the red light lane, where inspection days quietly add cost. The fourth is partner design: an operator with warehouses on both sides of the border removes handoffs, and each handoff removed is a place where cost and time leak out. None of these are tricks; they are just the parts of the process that a disciplined shipper controls.

How do 2026 tariff changes affect your cost?

If your goods are US origin, the 2026 decree does not raise your duty, which stays at 0 percent under the USMCA. If they are non treaty origin, such as from China, duty can now be 5 to 50 percent.

The 2026 tariff decree changed the cost picture sharply, but only for some shippers. Effective January 1, 2026, Mexico raised tariffs to between 10 and 50 percent on about 1,648 tariff lines total, after an April 2026 decree added 185 to the original 1,463, covering sectors like textiles, apparel, footwear, steel, and autos, and aimed at goods from countries without a free trade agreement, notably China. The decree runs through December 31, 2026 and may be extended. The key point for budgeting is origin. If your goods qualify as US origin under the USMCA, none of this applies and your duty stays at 0 percent on most products. If your goods are non treaty origin, the same product that shipped cheaply last year may now carry a substantial duty, which changes whether the Mexican market is profitable at your price. This is why many sellers are consolidating in the US to ship US origin, and why confirming origin and classification with your broker is now a pricing decision, not just a compliance step.

The 16% rate is set in the value added tax law, and importing goods is one of the listed taxable activities:

  • De minimis: The de minimis is the value below which US origin goods enter with no tax up to 50 dollars and no duty up to 117 dollars.
  • IVA: IVA is Mexico's value added tax, at a standard 16 percent, charged on imports.

The DTA is Mexico's customs processing fee. For general imports it is 0.8 percent of the customs value, but for USMCA operations it is a fixed amount of about 362 MXN per pedimento in 2026, updated quarterly. It is small but appears on almost every import.

translations.excerpt: You can sell on Amazon Mexico from the US with NARF, which ships from US inventory, or with FBA Mexico, which stocks locally. This guide compares both and covers the RFC and customs steps.
translations.content:
You can sell on Amazon Mexico from the US in two ways. With North America Remote Fulfillment (NARF), you list your US FBA inventory on amazon.com.mx and Amazon ships each order from the US, with the customer paying import fees at checkout. With FBA Mexico, you import inventory into Mexico for faster, cheaper local delivery, which needs an RFC and customs clearance. Both start with a professional selling account.

  • NARF lets you list US FBA inventory on amazon.com.mx and fulfill Mexico orders from the US, with the customer as importer of record (Amazon Seller Central).
  • With NARF, Prime delivery to Mexico typically takes 5 to 9 days, and a cross border NARF fee replaces the standard FBA fee (Amazon).
  • FBA Mexico stocks inventory locally for faster delivery but requires importing into Mexico, which needs a customs broker and an RFC.
  • Import IVA is 16 percent and US origin goods are 0 percent duty under the USMCA when you import in bulk (SAT, trade.gov).
  • A North America Unified Account lets you manage the US, Mexico, and Canada from one login (Amazon Seller Central).

How do I start selling on Amazon Mexico from the US?

Open a professional selling account on amazon.com.mx, usually through your North America Unified Account, list your products, then choose a fulfillment model: NARF from US inventory or FBA Mexico with local stock.

Getting onto Amazon Mexico from the US is more accessible than most sellers expect, because Amazon runs the US, Mexico, and Canada as one connected region. The starting point is a professional selling account on amazon.com.mx, which you can usually reach through a North America Unified Account so you manage all three countries from one login. You create or link your listings, adapt them into Spanish, and set prices in pesos. The real decision is fulfillment, and there are two clear paths. The first is North America Remote Fulfillment (NARF), where you keep your inventory in US FBA warehouses and Amazon ships each Mexican order across the border for you. The second is FBA Mexico, where you send inventory into Mexico ahead of time so orders ship locally. NARF is the low commitment way to test demand; FBA Mexico is the way to compete on speed and cost once demand is proven. Most successful sellers start with one and graduate to the other, and the logistics of importing bulk inventory is where a cross border partner comes in.

What is NARF and how does it work?

North America Remote Fulfillment lets you list US FBA inventory on amazon.com.mx. When a Mexican customer buys, Amazon ships from your US stock and the customer pays estimated import fees at checkout.

North America Remote Fulfillment, or NARF, is Amazon's way of letting you sell into Mexico without holding any inventory there. You enable it on your US FBA inventory, and your products appear on amazon.com.mx using a shared, or global, SKU, so the same stock is offered across the US, Mexico, and Canada. When a Mexican shopper buys, Amazon fulfills the order from your US warehouse and moves it across the border. The customer is the importer of record and pays the applicable import duties and taxes, which Amazon estimates and adds to the price at checkout as a deposit. In exchange for the convenience, a cross border NARF fee replaces the standard FBA fee, and Prime delivery to Mexico typically runs 5 to 9 days rather than next day. NARF is the fastest way to test whether Mexican demand exists for your catalog, because you risk no inventory and no local import. Its trade offs are slower delivery and thinner margins, which is exactly what FBA Mexico is designed to fix once you know a product sells.

What is FBA Mexico and when should you use it?

FBA Mexico means you import inventory into Mexico and store it in local fulfillment centers, so orders ship fast and cheap domestically. Use it once demand is proven and volume justifies importing in bulk.

FBA Mexico is the local model: instead of shipping each order from the US, you import inventory into Mexico in bulk and store it in Amazon's Mexican fulfillment centers, so orders ship domestically. The payoff is real. Delivery becomes fast local Prime rather than a 5 to 9 day cross border trip, per unit fulfillment fees are lower than the NARF fee, and returns are handled inside Mexico. The cost of that payoff is that you now import: you need a customs broker to file the pedimento, an RFC or an importer of record arrangement, and a plan to move the goods from the US into Mexico and on to the fulfillment centers. This is exactly the bulk cross border leg that an operator like BringGo Ship runs from Laredo and Monterrey, preparing the entry and delivering into the Amazon network. The rule of thumb is simple: use NARF to prove demand with no commitment, then switch a proven product to FBA Mexico once the volume makes the import worthwhile, because that is when local stock wins on both speed and margin.

NARF or FBA Mexico: how do you choose?

Choose NARF to test the market with no local inventory and no import. Choose FBA Mexico once a product sells steadily, because local stock delivers faster and cheaper per unit and justifies the import work.

The choice is really about commitment and proof. NARF asks almost nothing of you: no inventory in Mexico, no import, no RFC, because the customer clears the goods. That makes it the right first step for any product whose Mexican demand you are unsure of, and a sensible permanent home for slow or long tail items where holding local stock would not pay. Its costs are structural: delivery of 5 to 9 days is slower than local Prime, and the cross border fee compresses margin, so a NARF price often has to be higher. FBA Mexico flips both. Local stock ships fast, the per unit fee is lower, and returns stay in country, but you take on the import: broker, RFC or importer of record, and the freight to move bulk inventory across the border. The practical pattern is to run NARF first, watch which SKUs sell steadily, and migrate those to FBA Mexico while leaving the rest on NARF. You do not have to pick one model for your whole catalog; you match the model to each product's demand.

Do you need an RFC to sell on Amazon Mexico?

For NARF, no, because the customer is the importer of record. For FBA Mexico, you import in bulk, so you need an RFC or an importer of record partner and a customs broker to clear the goods.

Whether you need an RFC, the Mexican tax ID, depends entirely on your fulfillment model. Under NARF you do not import anything; the Mexican customer is the importer of record and pays the import fees at checkout, so you can sell without an RFC of your own. That is a large part of why NARF is the low friction entry. FBA Mexico is different, because you are importing bulk inventory into the country. That import needs a licensed customs broker to file the pedimento, and it needs an importer identity: either your own RFC and import registration, or a partner that acts as the importer of record and clears the goods in its name while you set up your own registration. Since January 2025 the importer's RFC is required on every declaration, so this is not a step you can skip. Sellers who plan to scale in Mexico usually start the RFC process early, because having it in place is what lets you move from testing on NARF to competing on FBA Mexico without a pause.

What are the taxes and duties on Amazon Mexico inventory?

IVA is 16 percent. For bulk imports under FBA Mexico, US origin goods are 0 percent duty under the USMCA. Under NARF, the customer pays estimated duties and taxes at checkout instead.

Tax treatment again follows the model. With NARF, you do not deal with Mexican import tax directly on each sale; Amazon estimates the duties and taxes and the customer pays them as a deposit at checkout as the importer of record. Your job there is pricing, because those added fees affect how competitive your listing looks. With FBA Mexico, you are the importer of the bulk shipment, so the normal import rules apply: IVA is 16 percent, and US origin goods enter at 0 percent duty on most products under the USMCA, which is a strong reason to source or consolidate in the US before importing. Goods of non treaty origin can face the 2026 tariffs of 5 to 50 percent on affected lines, which can change whether a product is viable in Mexico at your price. On top of the fiscal cost sit Amazon's own selling and fulfillment fees in pesos. The takeaway is to model the full cost for each model before you commit inventory, because a product that pencils out on FBA Mexico with US origin may not on NARF, and vice versa.

How do you get inventory into Mexico for FBA?

You ship bulk inventory across the border, clear customs with a broker, and deliver into Amazon's Mexican fulfillment centers. A cross border operator with warehouses on both sides runs this as one service.

Moving inventory into FBA Mexico is a standard cross border import with an Amazon delivery at the end, and it is the part where sellers most often want a partner. The flow is: consolidate your goods at a US warehouse, complete US export, transfer the trailer across the border, have a licensed broker clear the pedimento and pay duty and IVA, then deliver into Amazon's Mexican fulfillment centers under their receiving requirements. Each link matters, because Amazon has appointment and labeling rules on the receiving end, and a customs delay upstream can cause you to miss a delivery window. This is why an operator with warehouses on both sides of the border is useful: BringGo Ship consolidates in Laredo, prepares the entry file, and delivers into the Mexican network from its Monterrey side, so the import and the FBA delivery are one coordinated move rather than three vendors and two handoffs. For a seller, the value is not just the freight; it is that the inventory arrives cleared, compliant, and inside Amazon's window.

What are the most common mistakes selling on Amazon Mexico?

Pricing NARF listings as if there were no import fee, translating listings literally instead of adapting them, ignoring the RFC step for FBA, and importing without planning the customs and receiving windows.

A handful of avoidable mistakes cost new Amazon Mexico sellers the most. The first is pricing: under NARF the customer pays an import fee at checkout, so a price copied straight from the US can look uncompetitive once that fee is added, and sellers who do not adjust wonder why nothing sells. The second is language: running US listings through a literal translation instead of adapting them into natural Mexican Spanish hurts conversion and search visibility. The third is leaving the RFC and importer setup to the last minute, which stalls the move to FBA Mexico just when a product is taking off. The fourth is treating the import as an afterthought: shipping bulk inventory without planning the customs clearance and Amazon's receiving appointments leads to missed windows and stranded stock. None of these are hard to avoid. Price for the model, adapt the listing, start the RFC early, and plan the import and the FBA delivery together, ideally with a partner who has done the border leg before.
